docs.title: Mycelium
docs.text: Mycelium is an experimental library for generating stack graphs from source code using Tree-sitter. It is inspired by GitHub’s Stack Graphs implementation described in the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01224. The library is designed to replace Sourcegraph’s SCIP pipeline in Crader (formerly sheep-codebase-indexer) with a lighter, fully controlled semantic indexer.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Provide local semantic indexing without external infrastructure.
  • Enable precise control of language semantics via queries and handlers.
  • Deliver consistent integration for Crader and other internal tooling.
  • Offer debuggable output through visual inspection and deterministic builds.

docs.title: Current status
docs.text: Mycelium is in prototype stage. APIs and models are not yet stable and may change.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Mycelium implements a modular pipeline to generate stack graphs from Tree-sitter syntax trees.

docs.title: Pipeline overview
docs.text:
1. Parsing: Tree-sitter parses source code into a typed AST.
  2. Captures: Tree-sitter queries select relevant AST nodes.
  3. Handlers: language-specific handlers translate captures into semantic nodes.
  4. Graph Builder: combines handler output into a unified graph.
  5. Visualization: outputs HTML for inspection and debugging.

docs.title: src/captures.py
docs.text:
• Loads the requested Tree-sitter language.
  • Compiles multiple query strings into a single Query object.
  • Provides a dispatch map that binds capture names to handlers.

docs.title: src/graph.py
docs.text:
• Implements the GraphBuilder and stack-based processing.
  • Orders captures by byte range to preserve hierarchy.
  • Aggregates handler output into GNode structures.

docs.title: src/models.py
docs.text:
• Defines GNode, the core graph node abstraction.
  • Tracks symbol, type, ctx, and parent/child relationships.

docs.title: src/visualizer.py
docs.text:
• Produces standalone HTML for graph visualization.
  • Uses subgraph clusters to represent scope boundaries.
  • Applies distinct styling for PUSH/POP nodes.

docs.title: Architectural principles
docs.text:
• Separation of concerns: parsing, capturing, and building are distinct.
  • Extensibility: language support should be added without touching core modules.
  • Determinism: the graph builder must produce stable, repeatable output.
  • Integration-first design: output should be compatible with Crader expectations.

docs.title: Technical roadmap
docs.text:
• Multi-language coverage with validated query suites.
  • Stable node schema and serialization format.
  • Automated regression tests on curated corpora.
  • Performance profiling and memory optimization.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: This page summarizes the expected development workflow and quality standards for Mycelium.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Create a dedicated branch.
  2. Implement changes with small, focused commits.
  3. Update documentation and examples as needed.
  4. Run manual verification steps before submitting.

docs.title: Quality standards
docs.text:
• Readable code with explicit naming and minimal side effects.
  • Stable public APIs and documented behavior.
  • Minimal breaking changes unless explicitly justified.
  • Crader alignment for any semantic changes.

docs.title: Debugging & visualization
docs.text: The HTML visualizer in src/visualizer.py is the primary debugging tool for validating graph output. Use it after modifying queries or handlers.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide walks you through installing and running Mycelium locally.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10+ recommended.
  • pip or pipx.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
from tree_sitter import Parser
from src.captures import CapturesManager
from src.graph import GraphBuilder
from src.visualizer import visualize_graph

code = """
full_name = lambda first, last: f'Full name: {first.title()} {last.title()}'
full_name('guido', 'van rossum')
"""

manager = CapturesManager("python")
parser = Parser(manager.LANGUAGE)
root = parser.parse(code.encode("utf8")).root_node

captures = manager.execute(root)

builder = GraphBuilder()
roots = builder.build(captures, manager.get_handlers())

visualize_graph(roots)

Open graph.html in a browser to inspect the result.

docs.text:
A demo script is available in main.py:

python main.py

docs.title: Language Support
docs.text: Mycelium relies on Tree-sitter and a query/handler system that maps AST nodes into stack-graph nodes.

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text: Language Status Notes Python ✅ Prototype Queries in src/languages/python/queries.py

docs.title: Adding a new language
docs.text:
1. Add the Tree-sitter grammar package (e.g., tree-sitter-go).
  2. Create src/languages/<language>/.
  3. Implement queries.py with captures and handlers.
  4. Extend CapturesManager._load_language to load the new Language.
  5. Document the new language in this page and add usage notes.

docs.title: Query design guidelines
docs.text:
• Use stable and descriptive capture names.
  • Keep definitions and references in separate queries when possible.
  • Verify byte ranges to ensure correct ordering in the graph builder.
  • Prefer deterministic output over aggressive optimizations.

docs.title: Stack Graphs Concepts
docs.text: Stack graphs are a data structure for representing lexical scoping and name resolution at scale. Mycelium follows the principles described in GitHub’s Stack Graphs paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01224.

docs.title: Core objective
docs.text:
Represent the semantics of a codebase by modeling:

  • Definitions (symbol introductions).
  • References (symbol usages).
  • Scope boundaries and visibility rules.
  • Resolution paths from references to definitions.

docs.title: Key node types
docs.text:
• SCOPE: represents a lexical context (file, class, function, or block).
  • PUSH: introduces a symbol onto a resolution stack.
  • POP: resolves a symbol by matching against the stack.

In Mycelium, these are encoded as GNode instances with type and ctx fields.

docs.title: Practical implications
docs.text:
• Tree-sitter queries define which AST nodes participate in symbol resolution.
  • Handlers interpret syntax nodes and emit GNode structures.
  • The graph builder preserves ordering and hierarchy using byte ranges.
  • Accurate capture ordering is critical for deterministic name resolution.

docs.title: Why Stack Graphs (and why not SCIP)
docs.text: This page explains why stack graphs are a strong fit for Mycelium and why they are preferred over SCIP for Crader’s indexing pipeline.

docs.title: Performance foundations
docs.text:
Stack graphs were designed to support fast, incremental name resolution across large codebases. The model enables:

  • Partial paths: resolution can be computed by composing smaller path segments, avoiding full-graph traversal for every query.
  • Incremental updates: when a file changes, only the affected subgraph needs to be recomputed, not the entire index.
  • Composable resolution: stack effects are local and composable, enabling efficient cache reuse.
  • Deterministic ordering: byte-range ordering keeps graph construction stable and avoids expensive global re-sorting.

These properties reduce recomputation and allow the index to scale with fewer CPU and memory spikes than whole-project re-indexing.

docs.title: Why it’s faster than SCIP (in this context)
docs.text:
SCIP is a broad, language-server oriented indexing format. It excels as a universal interchange, but in Crader’s pipeline it introduces overhead that stack graphs can avoid:

  • Heavier schema & payload: SCIP includes rich metadata and cross-tool compatibility that is not always needed for internal indexing.
  • Full re-indexing pressure: SCIP workflows often favor rebuilding indexes or re-exporting large artifacts after changes.
  • Less control over resolution semantics: Mycelium requires tight control over scoping and resolution rules, which stack graphs allow through custom handlers.

By using stack graphs directly, Mycelium focuses on minimal semantic information required for resolution and indexing, which reduces I/O and computational overhead.

docs.title: Practical implications for Crader
docs.text:
• Faster incremental indexing of large monorepos.
  • Lower storage footprint for semantic data.
  • Greater control over language-specific name resolution.
  • Better alignment with custom analysis requirements.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Stack graphs provide a purpose-built model for scalable, incremental name resolution. For Crader’s use case, they deliver better performance characteristics and more controllable semantics than a general-purpose interchange format like SCIP.
